# Why This Page Exists

The linear mixed models lecture fits exactly one random effect —
`(1 | patch)`, a **random intercept**. That is the right place to start,
and it covers most nested designs. But two questions come up the moment
you have data collected **over time** or **along a gradient**:

1. What if the *relationship* differs from group to group, not just the
   baseline? → a **random slope**.
2. What if observations close together in time are more alike than
   observations far apart? → a **residual correlation structure**.

This page answers both, with runnable code. It is a reference, not a
lecture — read the section you need.

::: callout-important
## The two halves of a mixed model

Every mixed model specifies **two** variance-covariance matrices, and
people routinely confuse them:

$$\mathbf{V} = \underbrace{\mathbf{Z}\,\mathbf{G}\,\mathbf{Z}^\top}_{\text{random effects}} \;+\; \underbrace{\mathbf{R}}_{\text{residuals}}$$

- $\mathbf{G}$ — the variance-covariance of the **random effects**. This
  is what `(1 | g)` vs. `(1 + x | g)` changes.
- $\mathbf{R}$ — the variance-covariance of the **residuals**. By
  default $\mathbf{R} = \sigma^2\mathbf{I}$: equal variances, zero
  correlation. This is what `correlation =` and `weights =` change.

**`lme4` can only change $\mathbf{G}$.** To change $\mathbf{R}$ you need
`nlme` or `glmmTMB`. That single fact explains most of this page.
:::

## Setup

```{r mms-setup}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false

library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)   # Satterthwaite / Kenward-Roger df for lmer
library(nlme)       # residual correlation and variance structures
library(tidyverse)

options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))
```

::: callout-warning
## Load order matters

`nlme` and `lme4` both define `lmer`-adjacent generics, and both export
a function called `lmList`. Loading **`nlme` after `lme4`** (as above) is
the order that works for this page: `lmer()` still comes from `lme4`,
and `lme()`, `gls()`, `corAR1()` come from `nlme`. If anything behaves
oddly, call functions explicitly — `lme4::lmer()`, `nlme::lme()`.
:::

# Part 1 · Random Intercept Only

We will use `sleepstudy`, which ships with `lme4`: the average reaction
time of 18 subjects on each of 10 nights of restricted sleep. Eighteen
groups, ten observations each, perfectly balanced.

```{r data}
#| collapse: true
data(sleepstudy)
head(sleepstudy, 4)
```

A random intercept says: **every subject has their own baseline reaction
time, but sleep deprivation costs everybody the same amount per night.**

```{r m-int}
#| collapse: true
m_int <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), data = sleepstudy)

VarCorr(m_int)
fixef(m_int)
```

$$\text{Reaction}_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Days}_{ij} + b_{0i} + \epsilon_{ij},
\qquad b_{0i} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\text{int}})$$

One extra variance, `r round(as.data.frame(VarCorr(m_int))$sdcor[1], 1)`²,
is all the random effect costs. Read the fit as **18 parallel lines** —
different heights, identical slope of
`r round(fixef(m_int)[2], 2)` ms per night.

```{r fig-parallel}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "Reaction time against days of sleep deprivation for eighteen subjects, with the random-intercept model's fitted lines drawn for each subject. All eighteen lines are parallel and differ only in height."
sleepstudy$fit_int <- fitted(m_int)

ggplot(sleepstudy, aes(Days, Reaction, group = Subject)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit_int), alpha = 0.7, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Days of sleep deprivation", y = "Reaction time (ms)",
       title = "(1 | Subject): parallel lines") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

::: callout-note
## When a random intercept is enough

- The groups are **nesting units**, not things you measured a slope in —
  patches, tanks, litters, plots.
- You have one predictor level per group (every quadrat in a patch got
  the same treatment), so there is **no within-group slope to estimate**.
  This is the sea urchin case: `treat` does not vary inside a patch, so
  `(1 + treat | patch)` is not even estimable.
:::

# Part 2 · Random Intercept **and** Random Slope

Now allow each subject their own *response* to sleep loss:

```{r m-slope}
#| collapse: true
m_slope <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 + Days | Subject), data = sleepstudy)

VarCorr(m_slope)
```

$$\text{Reaction}_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Days}_{ij} + b_{0i} + b_{1i}\text{Days}_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij}$$

$$\begin{pmatrix} b_{0i} \\ b_{1i} \end{pmatrix} \sim
N\!\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix},\;
\mathbf{G} = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma^2_{\text{int}} & \rho\,\sigma_{\text{int}}\sigma_{\text{slope}} \\
\rho\,\sigma_{\text{int}}\sigma_{\text{slope}} & \sigma^2_{\text{slope}} \end{pmatrix} \right)$$

`VarCorr()` now prints **three** numbers, not one: an intercept SD, a
slope SD, and the **correlation between them**. That correlation is the
off-diagonal of $\mathbf{G}$ — it asks *do subjects who start slow also
deteriorate fastest?*

```{r coef-slope}
#| collapse: true
head(coef(m_slope)$Subject, 5)   # each subject's own intercept and slope
```

```{r fig-slopes}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "Reaction time against days of sleep deprivation for eighteen subjects with the random-slope model's fitted lines. The lines now fan out, differing in steepness as well as height, with one subject nearly flat and another rising steeply."
sleepstudy$fit_slope <- fitted(m_slope)

ggplot(sleepstudy, aes(Days, Reaction, group = Subject)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit_slope), alpha = 0.7, color = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "Days of sleep deprivation", y = "Reaction time (ms)",
       title = "(1 + Days | Subject): lines fan out") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

::: callout-tip
## Reading the formula, every time

$$(\ \text{what varies}\ \mid\ \text{across what}\ )$$

| Formula | $\mathbf{G}$ is | Parameters in $\mathbf{G}$ |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| `(1 \| g)` | 1 × 1 | 1 variance |
| `(1 + x \| g)` | 2 × 2, correlated | 2 variances + 1 correlation = **3** |
| `(1 + x + z \| g)` | 3 × 3 | 3 variances + 3 correlations = **6** |
| `(0 + x \| g)` | 1 × 1 | 1 variance (slope only, shared intercept) |

`1 + x` is the default, so `(x \| g)` and `(1 + x \| g)` are the **same
model**. Write the `1` anyway — it is what reminds you the intercept is
in there.
:::

::: callout-warning
## Random slopes get expensive fast

A random slope for every predictor is a $k \times k$ matrix with
$k(k+1)/2$ parameters. Three random slopes plus an intercept is **10**
variance parameters estimated from however many groups you have. This is
the single most common cause of `boundary (singular) fit` — the model is
asking the data for more than it contains. Keep the random-effects
structure as simple as the design allows.
:::

# Part 3 · Correlated vs. Uncorrelated Slopes

By default `lme4` estimates the intercept-slope correlation. You can
forbid it, which saves a parameter:

```{r m-uncorr}
#| collapse: true
m_corr   <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 + Days | Subject), sleepstudy)

m_uncorr <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject) + (0 + Days | Subject),
                 sleepstudy)

m_dbar   <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (Days || Subject), sleepstudy)

VarCorr(m_corr)
VarCorr(m_uncorr)
```

`m_uncorr` and `m_dbar` are the same model — `||` is shorthand for
splitting the term. Here the estimated correlation is tiny, so dropping
it changes almost nothing and buys back a df.

::: callout-warning
## `||` does not do what you expect with a **factor**

`(f \|\| g)` does **not** decorrelate the levels of a factor `f` — it
expands `f` into one term, not one per level. For a factor you need
`afex::mixed`'s `expand_re = TRUE`, or `(1 \| g) + (0 + dummy(f, "b") \| g)`
written out by hand. With a **numeric** predictor, as here, `||` works
exactly as advertised.
:::

# Part 4 · Choosing Between Them

```{r compare-re}
#| collapse: true
# RANDOM effects: compare with REML, which is the default.
# refit = FALSE stops anova() from silently refitting with ML.
anova(m_int, m_uncorr, m_corr, refit = FALSE)
```

The jump from `m_int` to `m_uncorr` is enormous — the random slope is
real. The further jump to `m_corr` is worth nothing, so the
intercept–slope correlation is not supported here.

```{r compare-fixed}
#| collapse: true
# FIXED effects: refit with ML first. REML likelihoods from models with
# different fixed effects are NOT comparable.
m0 <- lmer(Reaction ~ 1    + (1 + Days | Subject), sleepstudy, REML = FALSE)
m1 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 + Days | Subject), sleepstudy, REML = FALSE)
anova(m0, m1)

# or, better for a small sample, the F-test with adjusted denominator df
anova(m_slope)
```

::: callout-important
## Three rules for comparing mixed models

1. **Different random effects, same fixed effects** → compare with
   **REML** (`refit = FALSE`).
2. **Different fixed effects** → compare with **ML** (`REML = FALSE`),
   or better, don't do an LRT at all — use the Kenward-Roger or
   Satterthwaite *F*-test.
3. The LRT *p*-value for dropping a **variance** is **conservative**.
   The null sits on the boundary (σ² = 0), so the test statistic is not
   really χ²₁ — it is a 50:50 mixture of χ²₀ and χ²₁. Halve the
   *p*-value, or use `RLRsim::exactRLRT()`, if you are near the line.
:::

::: callout-tip
## Keep it maximal, but keep it fitting

The common advice (Barr et al. 2013) is to include a random slope for
**every predictor that varies within a group** — the "maximal" model —
because omitting one inflates Type I error for that fixed effect.
The counter-argument (Bates et al. 2015) is that maximal models often
do not converge and cost power. A workable compromise: start maximal,
and if you get a singular fit, drop correlations first (`||`), then the
least-supported slope, and **report what you dropped and why**.
:::

# Part 5 · Changing the Residual Matrix — Why You Need `nlme`

Everything so far changed $\mathbf{G}$. Now for $\mathbf{R}$.

`lmer()` hard-codes $\mathbf{R} = \sigma^2\mathbf{I}$: every residual has
the same variance and no two residuals are correlated. For repeated
measures that is often wrong on **both** counts. `nlme::lme()` lets you
set $\mathbf{R}$ with two arguments:

- `correlation =` — the **correlation** part of $\mathbf{R}$
- `weights =` — the **variance** part of $\mathbf{R}$

We switch datasets to something with a real time axis: `Loblolly`, which
ships with base R — the height of 14 loblolly pine seed sources measured
at ages 3, 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 years. Fourteen groups, six times each,
balanced, and **unevenly spaced in time**, which will matter.

```{r lob}
#| collapse: true
data(Loblolly)
lob <- as.data.frame(Loblolly)
str(lob)
table(table(lob$Seed))        # 14 seed sources, 6 measurements each
sort(unique(lob$age))
```

```{r fig-lob}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-alt: "Height of fourteen loblolly pine seed sources plotted against age from 3 to 25 years, one line per seed source. All lines rise steeply and nearly straight, and the spread between seed sources widens with age."
ggplot(lob, aes(age, height, group = Seed)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) + geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Age (yr)", y = "Height (ft)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

The baseline model, the `nlme` equivalent of `lmer(height ~ age + (1|Seed))`:

```{r l-ri}
#| collapse: true
ctrl <- lmeControl(opt = "optim", msMaxIter = 200)

l_ri <- lme(height ~ age, random = ~ 1 | Seed, data = lob, control = ctrl)

# nlme syntax map:
#   lmer(y ~ x + (1     | g))  ->  lme(y ~ x, random = ~ 1     | g)
#   lmer(y ~ x + (1 + x | g))  ->  lme(y ~ x, random = ~ 1 + x | g)
#   lmer(y ~ x + (1|a) + (1|b)) -> lme(y ~ x, random = list(a = ~1, b = ~1))
#                                   ... for NESTED a/b only; nlme cannot do
#                                   crossed random effects. Use lme4 for those.
VarCorr(l_ri)
```

::: callout-note
## Is my residual correlation real? Look first.

```{r acf}
#| collapse: true
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-alt: "Autocorrelation function of the within-group residuals from the random-intercept model, plotted against lag 0 to 4, with a dashed significance band; the lag-1 autocorrelation is positive and the lag-2 and lag-3 values are negative and outside the band."
ACF(l_ri, maxLag = 4)
plot(ACF(l_ri, maxLag = 4), alpha = 0.05)
```

`ACF()` on an `lme` fit is the diagnostic: it computes the
autocorrelation of the **within-group** residuals at each lag. Points
outside the band mean the independence assumption built into
$\mathbf{R}$ is violated.

Keep `maxLag` well below the number of observations per group. With 6
measurements per tree, lag 5 rests on **one pair per group** and is
noise.
:::

::: callout-warning
## Serial correlation is often a misspecified **mean**, not correlated noise

Notice the lag-1 value is positive and lag 2–3 are negative. That is the
signature of fitting a **straight line to a curve**: the residuals are
systematically high in the middle and low at the ends, and an ACF reads
that as correlation.

Before you buy an AR(1), ask whether the fix is actually a better mean
structure — `poly(age, 2)`, a log transform, a spline, or a nonlinear
growth model (`nlme::nlme()`). An AR(1) bolted onto the wrong curve
makes the *p*-values look better without making the model right. On
this dataset both are arguably true, which is why it is a good teaching
example and a bad final analysis.
:::

# Part 6 · Time-Series Correlation Structures

## AR(1) — the workhorse

An autoregressive-1 structure says the correlation between two residuals
decays geometrically with how far apart they are:

$$\mathbf{R} = \sigma^2
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & \phi & \phi^2 & \phi^3 \\
\phi & 1 & \phi & \phi^2 \\
\phi^2 & \phi & 1 & \phi \\
\phi^3 & \phi^2 & \phi & 1
\end{pmatrix}$$

**One** parameter, $\phi$, for a matrix of any size. That is why it is
the default choice for time series.

```{r l-ar1}
#| collapse: true
l_ar1 <- lme(height ~ age, random = ~ 1 | Seed, data = lob,
             correlation = corAR1(form = ~ 1 | Seed), control = ctrl)

# the estimated phi
coef(l_ar1$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)

# the 6x6 residual correlation matrix the model is now using
round(corMatrix(l_ar1$modelStruct$corStruct)[[1]], 3)
```

::: callout-important
## Read `form =` carefully — it is the whole thing

`correlation = corAR1(form = ~ time | group)`

- **right of the `|`** — the grouping. Residuals in *different* groups
  are independent. Almost always the same grouping as your random
  effect.
- **left of the `|`** — the **time variable**, which must be a
  **position index**: `corAR1` raises $\phi$ to the power of the
  *difference in position*, and assumes successive positions are equally
  spaced.
- `form = ~ 1 | g` means "use row order within the group". Fine **only**
  if the rows are sorted by time and nothing is missing. Being explicit
  (`form = ~ visit | g`) is safer.
:::

## `corCAR1` — when the times are not equally spaced

Our ages are 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. The gap from 3 to 5 is two years; the
gap from 20 to 25 is five. `corAR1` with `form = ~ 1 | Seed` treats both
as "one step apart", which is wrong. `corCAR1` uses the actual value:
$\text{cor} = \phi^{|t_i - t_j|}$ for continuous $t$.

```{r l-car1}
#| collapse: true
l_car1 <- lme(height ~ age, random = ~ 1 | Seed, data = lob,
              correlation = corCAR1(form = ~ age | Seed), control = ctrl)

coef(l_car1$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)
```

::: callout-warning
## `corAR1` needs an **integer** time variable — and fails silently

`corAR1` requires the variable left of the `|` to be a consecutive
integer sequence. Hand it `age` and it does **not** error:

```{r ar1-trap}
#| collapse: true
l_wrong <- lme(height ~ age, random = ~ 1 | Seed, data = lob,
               correlation = corAR1(form = ~ age | Seed), control = ctrl)

coef(l_wrong$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)
```

φ comes back as **exactly 0** — the structure quietly switched itself
off, and you would have reported "no autocorrelation" from a model that
found φ = 0.55 when asked properly. Either pass a true index
(`form = ~ 1 | Seed` on time-sorted data, or a `visit` column numbered
1, 2, 3 …) or use `corCAR1`, which is built for real-valued time.
**Always print the estimated φ.**
:::

## The rest of the catalogue

```{r l-others}
#| collapse: true
# compound symmetry: ONE correlation for every pair of times, any distance
l_cs <- lme(height ~ age, random = ~ 1 | Seed, data = lob,
            correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | Seed), control = ctrl)

# ARMA(1,1): an AR part and a moving-average part
l_arma <- lme(height ~ age, random = ~ 1 | Seed, data = lob,
              correlation = corARMA(form = ~ 1 | Seed, p = 1, q = 1),
              control = ctrl)
```

```{r cs-trap}
#| collapse: true
anova(l_ri, l_cs)
```

::: callout-important
## Compound symmetry adds **nothing** to a random intercept

The log-likelihoods are **identical** and the LRT statistic is zero.
This is not a bug and it is worth understanding, because it is the
cleanest illustration of $\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{ZGZ}^\top + \mathbf{R}$:

A random intercept already *implies* compound symmetry. Two
observations in the same group share $b_{0i}$, so

$$\text{cor} = \frac{\sigma^2_{\text{int}}}{\sigma^2_{\text{int}} + \sigma^2} = \text{ICC}$$

for **every** pair, regardless of distance. `(1 | Seed)` and
`corCompSymm` are two notations for the same matrix, and fitting both
makes the model unidentifiable — `nlme` just puts the whole thing in one
of the two terms.

**So: the reason to reach for AR(1) is not that you have grouped data —
the random intercept already handled that. It is that you believe
observations close in time are *more* alike than observations far
apart.** A random intercept cannot express that. AR(1) can.
:::

## Comparing them

```{r compare-cor}
#| collapse: true
AIC(l_ri, l_cs, l_ar1, l_car1, l_arma)
```

These are not all nested in one another, so this is an AIC comparison,
not a sequence of LRTs. The ordering is the story:

- `l_cs` is worse than `l_ri` **only** by the 2 points its redundant
  extra parameter costs.
- `l_ar1` is a large improvement — there **is** serial correlation.
- `l_car1` is better still, because it uses the real age gaps.
- `l_arma` is best here, but with 14 groups be suspicious of the third
  correlation parameter before you report it.

::: callout-note
## Structures available in `nlme`

| Call | $\mathbf{R}$ structure | Parameters |
|-------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| *(default)* | independent, equal variance | 1 (σ²) |
| `corCompSymm` | compound symmetry / exchangeable | 2 |
| `corAR1` | AR(1), equally spaced integer time | 2 |
| `corCAR1` | continuous-time AR(1) | 2 |
| `corARMA(p, q)` | ARMA | 2 + *p* + *q* |
| `corSymm` | unstructured ("general") | 1 + *t*(*t*−1)/2 |
| `corExp`, `corGaus`, `corSpher`, `corLin`, `corRatio` | **spatial** — decay with 2-D distance; `form = ~ x + y \| g` | 2–3 |

The spatial ones are the same idea with distance in place of time, and
are how you handle spatially autocorrelated residuals.
:::

## Unstructured — estimate every correlation

The opposite extreme: no assumption at all, one parameter per pair of
times. With 6 times that is 15 correlations plus 6 variances.

```{r l-un}
#| collapse: true
l_un <- gls(height ~ age, data = lob,
            correlation = corSymm(form = ~ 1 | Seed),
            weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | age),
            control = glsControl(opt = "optim"))

round(corMatrix(l_un$modelStruct$corStruct)[[1]], 3)
```

::: callout-warning
## Unstructured needs a lot of data

$t(t-1)/2$ correlations from *n* groups. With 6 times and 14 seed
sources we are estimating 15 correlations from 14 groups — the numbers
above are not to be trusted, and they are near 1 because this is a
growth curve, not because the trees are interchangeable. Rule of thumb:
you want **many more groups than correlation parameters**. If not, use
AR(1).

Note also that `gls()` has **no random effect** — with an unstructured
$\mathbf{R}$ you usually drop the random intercept, since compound
symmetry is already a special case of unstructured (see the trap above).
:::

# Part 7 · Unequal Variances

The other half of $\mathbf{R}$. The Loblolly figure fans out with age,
so a single σ² is clearly wrong.

```{r l-var}
#| collapse: true
# one residual variance per age (a "variance group")
l_vi <- lme(height ~ age, random = ~ 1 | Seed, data = lob,
            weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | age), control = ctrl)

# variance as a smooth power of the fitted value: Var = sigma^2 * |mu|^(2*delta)
l_vp <- lme(height ~ age, random = ~ 1 | Seed, data = lob,
            weights = varPower(), control = ctrl)

AIC(l_ri, l_vi, l_vp)
anova(l_ri, l_vp)
```

Both are massive improvements — a single σ² was badly wrong. `varIdent`
wins on AIC here (it spends 5 extra parameters and uses them), but
`varPower` gets most of the way on **one** parameter, and unlike
`varIdent` it extrapolates to ages you did not measure. With a
continuous trend like this one, prefer `varPower`; reserve `varIdent`
for a handful of genuinely discrete groups.

::: callout-note
## Variance functions in `nlme`

| Call | Models | Use when |
|-------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| `varIdent(form = ~ 1 \| f)` | one σ² per level of `f` | a few discrete groups with obviously different spread |
| `varPower()` | σ²·\|μ\|^2δ | spread grows with the mean |
| `varExp()` | σ²·e^(2δμ) | spread grows faster than a power |
| `varConstPower()` | σ²(δ₁+\|μ\|^δ₂)² | spread grows but is nonzero at μ = 0 |
| `varFixed(~ x)` | σ²·x | you know the weights (e.g. group sizes) |

These combine: `weights = varPower()` **and**
`correlation = corCAR1(...)` in the same call is normal and often
necessary.
:::

# Which Package Do I Use?

::: callout-important
| I need | `lme4` | `nlme` | `glmmTMB` |
|-----------------|-----------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| Random intercepts and slopes | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| **Crossed** random effects | ✅ fast | ❌ nested only | ✅ |
| Thousands of groups | ✅ fast | slow | ✅ |
| Residual correlation (AR1, …) | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ (`ar1()`, `ou()`, `exp()`) |
| Unequal residual variance | ❌ | ✅ `weights =` | ✅ `dispformula =` |
| Non-normal response | `glmer()` | ❌ | ✅ best support |
| Zero inflation | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Kenward-Roger *F*-tests | ✅ `pbkrtest` | ❌ containment df only | ❌ |
:::

**A practical decision rule.** Nested or crossed grouping and nothing
special about the residuals → **`lme4`**. Repeated measures over time, or
unequal variances, with a normal response → **`nlme`**. Anything
non-normal, zero-inflated, or needing both a correlation structure *and*
crossed random effects → **`glmmTMB`**.

::: callout-tip
## `glmmTMB` equivalents, for reference

`glmmTMB` writes a residual correlation structure as an extra random
term, with the time variable as a **factor**:

``` r
library(glmmTMB)

# AR(1) residuals within Seed
glmmTMB(height ~ age + (1 | Seed) + ar1(factor(age) + 0 | Seed), data = lob)

# Ornstein-Uhlenbeck: continuous-time AR(1), the corCAR1 analogue
glmmTMB(height ~ age + ou(factor(age) + 0 | Seed), data = lob)

# unstructured
glmmTMB(height ~ age + us(factor(age) + 0 | Seed), data = lob)

# unequal residual variance by age
glmmTMB(height ~ age + (1 | Seed), dispformula = ~ factor(age), data = lob)
```

The `+ 0` matters — it drops the intercept from that term so you get one
level per time point. `glmmTMB` is not installed on the lab machines;
install it with `install.packages("glmmTMB")` if you want to try these.
:::

# Common Errors and What They Mean

::: callout-warning
**`boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')`**

A variance or correlation hit the edge of its range — a variance of
exactly 0, or a correlation of exactly ±1. Your random-effects structure
asks for more than the data support. Drop the correlation (`||`), then
the least-supported slope. Do not ignore it.
:::

::: callout-warning
**`Model failed to converge with max|grad| ...`**

Usually benign if small (< 0.01) and the estimates look sane. Try
scaling your predictors (`scale(x)`) — wildly different predictor scales
are the usual cause — or a different optimizer:
`control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")`.
:::

::: callout-warning
**`Error ... nlminb problem, convergence error code = 1` (nlme)**

`nlme`'s default optimizer is fragile with correlation structures. Pass
`control = lmeControl(opt = "optim", msMaxIter = 200)`, as every `lme()`
call on this page does.
:::

::: callout-warning
**`number of levels of each grouping factor must be < number of observations`**

You have asked for a random effect with one group per row. That variance
is not identifiable separately from the residual. Either drop it or
model it as the residual.
:::

# The One-Page Summary

::: callout-important
## $\mathbf{G}$ — the random effects (`lme4` or `nlme`)

``` r
(1     | g)   # random intercept:   parallel lines
(1 + x | g)   # intercept + slope:  lines fan out, correlated
(1 | g) + (0 + x | g)   # same, correlation forced to 0
(x || g)      # shorthand for the line above (numeric x only)
(0 + x | g)   # slope only, shared intercept
(1 | a/b)     # b nested in a  ==  (1|a) + (1|a:b)
(1 | a) + (1 | b)   # a and b crossed
```

## $\mathbf{R}$ — the residuals (`nlme` or `glmmTMB`)

``` r
lme(y ~ x, random = ~ 1 | g, data = d,
    correlation = corCAR1(form = ~ time | g),   # correlation part
    weights     = varPower(),                   # variance part
    control     = lmeControl(opt = "optim"))
```

**Diagnose before you prescribe:** `plot(ACF(fit), alpha = 0.05)` for
serial correlation, residuals-vs-fitted for unequal variance. Then
compare candidate structures by **AIC under REML with identical fixed
effects**.
:::

# Readings

- **Pinheiro, J. C., & Bates, D. M.** (2000). *Mixed-Effects Models in
  S and S-PLUS*. Springer. §5.3 is the definitive account of `nlme`'s
  `correlation =` and `weights =` arguments.
- **Zuur, A. F., Ieno, E. N., Walker, N. J., Saveliev, A. A., & Smith,
  G. M.** (2009). *Mixed Effects Models and Extensions in Ecology with
  R*. Springer. Ch. 6–7 — temporal and spatial correlation in ecological
  data, worked in `nlme`.
- **Bates, D., Mächler, M., Bolker, B., & Walker, S.** (2015). Fitting
  linear mixed-effects models using lme4. *Journal of Statistical
  Software, 67*(1), 1–48.
- **Barr, D. J., Levy, R., Scheepers, C., & Tily, H. J.** (2013). Random
  effects structure for confirmatory hypothesis testing: Keep it
  maximal. *Journal of Memory and Language, 68*(3), 255–278.
- **Brooks, M. E., et al.** (2017). glmmTMB balances speed and
  flexibility among packages for zero-inflated generalized linear mixed
  modeling. *The R Journal, 9*(2), 378–400.
